title: The Writing Revolution in Middle School
author: Erin Hanrahan
summary: Erin Hanrahan, a middle school ELA teacher, describes using The Writing Revolution's Because-But-So exercise to help students move beyond simple statements of preference and craft complex claims. Before a fishbowl discussion on whether the narrator of the historical fiction novel Chains should spy for the Patriots, students drafted three possible claims from one prompt instead of a single claim. They quickly had three complex ideas about the text, chose a favorite to gather evidence around, and brought it to the discussion. The result was a more nuanced conversation in which students probed one another's analysis with more "why" questions. She also recounts a department debate over TWR's use of "topic sentence" rather than "claim," and reports that TWR's chatbot explained the choice as sequencing vocabulary to match students' developing understanding of paragraph structure. Her experiment strengthened her conviction that a strong claim matters for reading, writing, speaking and listening alike.
points: Because-But-So asks students to expand a kernel sentence three times, which forces three distinct ideas about one topic.
Drafting three candidate claims before a discussion moved students past a binary spy or do-not-spy debate into the nuances of their positions.
As in all TWR work, the content of the kernel sentence drives the rigor, so an easy prompt like "Mondays are the worst" can be used to teach the routine before applying it to the novel.
TWR prefers "topic sentence" early to teach paragraph architecture, which the author reads as a matter of sequencing vocabulary, not of dismissing the claim.
Stronger claims raised the bar for both classroom discourse and the writing that followed.
quotes: Every year, I struggle to help students move beyond simple statements of preference and craft complex claims that provide a road map for the paragraph or ideas that follow.
One of the many versatile exercises TWR offers is Because-But-So, in which students expand a kernel sentence three times, adding each conjunction in turn and completing the sentence.
And, as always with TWR, the content of the kernel sentence drives the rigor of the exercise.
But instead of drafting one claim to answer the question, they used a Because-But-So prompt to draft three possible claims.
Instead of a binary discussion around whether Isabel should spy or not, students were able to move into the nuances of their claims.
students need to understand the architecture of a paragraph and the structural role of a topic sentence before they can tackle the rhetorical nuance of a claim.
A claim is an original idea, which is both the seed and the fruit of analysis. Strong claims boosted our discourse, and set a higher bar for the writing that followed as well.
